cited_by.title: Alpha-thalassaemia trait: small red cells that are not low iron

record.population: 1,491 African American and 31,005 white people with routine blood results and stored samples, about half men and half women
record.design: Retrospective analysis of laboratory data with DNA testing for the -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion
record.finding: Haematocrit, haemoglobin, MCV, transferrin saturation and white cell count were lower in African Americans; ferritin was higher. The -3.7 kb alpha-thalassaemia deletion accounted for about one third of the haemoglobin difference; sickle trait and raised creatinine had no effect. Of women, 19.8% of African Americans and 5.3% of white women would be called anaemic; without iron-deficient or thalassaemic people the figures were 6.1% and 2.77% (men 17.7% and 7.6%, then 4.29% and 3.6%). The authors say the same reference standards do not apply to all ethnic groups.
record.note: US laboratory population, not a random community sample. Abstract read in full. The authors favour separate standards; whether to adopt them is contested.

record.design: Analysis of anonymised laboratory data on haemoglobin, MCV, transferrin saturation, ferritin and white cell count
record.finding: Haemoglobin, haematocrit and MCV were lower in African-Americans. Among all subjects 19.8% of African-American women would be classed as anaemic against 5.3% of White women; after removing iron-deficient and thalassaemic subjects the gap narrowed to 6.1% and 2.77%. The alpha-thalassaemia deletion explained about a third of the haemoglobin difference. The authors say the same reference standards do not apply to all ethnic groups.
record.note: Laboratory-referred samples, not a population survey. A good example of a measured variable (alpha-thalassaemia deletion) standing behind a race difference.
